This paper introduces a novel time-dependent Poisson autoregression model designed to capture both mean and volatility clustering in count data. We establish the model's theoretical properties, proving the existence and uniqueness of its solution and deriving its asymptotic characteristics. Furthermore, we develop a simple iterative algorithm for estimation and conduct a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the estimator's asymptotic behavior. The study concludes with an empirical investigation into the financial returns of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Litecoin, followed by a comparison against other count data models. Additional findings regarding the practical utility of the proposed model for forecasting and risk management are also presented. The underlying mathematical framework relies on the theory of positive linear operators acting on the space of Borel measures over the non-negative real line. Specifically, the analysis utilizes the mean measure approach, which has been a standard method for investigating the asymptotic properties of stationary solutions in linear and nonlinear auto-regressive models for Gaussian and count data. Distinct from previous research, this work investigates the asymptotic behavior of the least squares estimator under this same framework. We introduce a robust and effective method for sampling the conformational space of organic molecules using the Langevin dynamics algorithm. This approach surpasses the efficacy of simulated annealing, a technique we also present in this report. The proposed method is straightforward to implement and requires no prior knowledge of the system's conformational landscape. Automated systems generating image captions are typically assessed using human-written reference data, such as the Flickr-8K, Flickr-22K, Instagram-146K, Visual Genome, and VIG datasets. The prevailing assumption is that these datasets offer an ideal gold standard for both evaluation and selection of descriptive methods. However, because these datasets consist of subjective human opinions rather than objective facts, they introduce inherent noise into the assessment process. This noise can mask genuine improvements or create illusions of progress where none exist. To address this issue, we introduce a metric called ROCAUD, which evaluates image description methods directly against the data distribution using a ranking approach, similar to AUC. This metric considers both correct and incorrect references, rendering it independent of specific reference selections. We also propose a set of baseline methods and conduct experiments across three standard datasets: Flickr-8K, Flickr-22K, and Visual Genome. Our analysis of the human benchmark data reveals significant inconsistencies, which we attribute to four primary causes. Furthermore, we present a dataset that ensures each image has only one reference per category, guaranteeing consistency; we utilize this data to define an ideal method for specific categories and demonstrate that current state-of-the-art approaches fail to meet this standard. Our findings indicate that the variability in existing image description datasets is far greater than anticipated, and that simply optimizing for these datasets is insufficient for creating truly effective image description methods. To facilitate future research, we release the consistent multi-reference image description dataset we developed, along with the necessary code and the ROCAUD metric, available at https://github.com/rohitgupta10/ROCAUD.

This study presents a self-consistent framework for predicting the properties of known and yet-to-be-discovered hadrons, with the objective of establishing a comprehensive "periodic table" of hadronic matter. The approach relies on the concept of diquark-diatet mesons and employs a novel, non-perturbative method to estimate the masses of single- and multi-quark hadrons. Central to this framework is the determination of the strong coupling constant, $\alpha_s$, as a function of the inter-diquark separation $r$. By assuming a constant value for $\alpha_s$ at a specific separation $r_0$ to calculate the masses of certain baryons and mesons, the model extrapolates this same constant to forecast the properties of other baryons and mesons. Furthermore, the framework predicts the masses of exotic hadrons through the addition of a di-diatet meson ($dd^{\ast}$) and a single diatet meson ($d^{\ast}$) to conventional quark-diatet ($qd$) and diquark ($d$) structures. Utilizing a constant $\alpha_s = 0.52$ at a separation of $r_0 = 0.35$ fm, the model successfully accounts for the spectrum of all single-hadrons, with predicted masses aligning closely with experimental data and other theoretical predictions. Beyond single-hadrons, the framework extends to predict the properties of multi-hadron systems, including $dd^{\ast}$-mesic baryons, $dd^{\ast}$-mesic mesons, and $dd^{\ast}$-nuclear states. These predictions are derived by considering a attractive Yukawa-like potential acting between the separating $\alpha_s$-diquark and diatet components. Overall, this work offers a unified model capable of predicting the properties of both single- and multi-hadron systems.

Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates diverse data sources, ranging from direct measurements to indirect ones derived via fitting procedures. This report outlines such a framework, detailing how to incorporate data processed through fitting steps. We present a unified framework capable of integrating all data types, including those obtained from prior fits. While this approach introduces additional uncertainties, it ensures consistency by utilizing the same theoretical structure for both direct data and those from earlier fits. We describe the implementation of this framework within the fastNLO code and demonstrate its application using a dataset from the LHCf experiment. Furthermore, we integrate data from other experiments that have been processed through previous workflows, such as the CT18 and MMHT2019 fits. The framework is also suitable for analyzing other data sources, whether direct or indirect, and can be employed to investigate the uncertainties associated with PDFs resulting from successive fitting procedures. Ultimately, this theory framework enables the incorporation of all available data types—direct and indirect—into a single global fit, thereby ensuring uniformity and consistency across the data selection. Such a unified framework is essential for generating PDF sets like the nXQCD family. To facilitate this goal, we have developed an open-source implementation of the framework in the fastNLO code, which is accessible at https://github.com/egavardi/fastNLO.

This study employs a linearized model to examine how a turbulent methane-air jet flame reacts to acoustic plane waves within a rectangular duct. The research begins with an overview of the linearized framework utilized to describe the interaction between the flame and acoustic plane waves. Subsequently, the study introduces an active flame model designed to simulate the response of the turbulent jet to acoustic forcing. The paper details the derivation of boundary conditions for both the passive and active components of the flow, velocity, and species gradients at the inlet. Furthermore, it outlines the methodology for determining these gradients via a linearized Recurrence Relation (RRC) approach. The study concludes by presenting results that validate the linearized model against direct numerical simulations of the flame's reaction to acoustic forcing, as well as against a non-linear RRC simulation subjected to a strong inlet disturbance. Finally, the research investigates the flame's reaction to acoustic plane waves across a range of frequencies, analyzing the corresponding acoustic modes and identifying the frequencies at which resonances occur. The linearized models for both the passive and active flow, velocity, and species gradients are implemented using a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) method for spatial discretization and an RRC approach for temporal discretization. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AdrienBouquet/LinearizedModels.

Nonlocal gravity represents a recent reformulation of Einstein's theory of general relativity, offering a framework where gravitational effects are described constitutively, mirroring the approach used in nonlocal elasticity for materials. This theory has already demonstrated significant potential in addressing longstanding challenges in astrophysics and cosmology, such as the stability of white dwarfs and neutrons stars, as well as the acceleration of cosmic expansion. Despite these advantages, the theory currently lacks a unified formulation that covers both linear and nonlinear aspects. Furthermore, existing literature has not yet fully explored the constitutive models required to account for nonlocal gravitational phenomena. In this work, we present a comprehensive formulation of nonlocal gravity that integrates both linear and nonlinear components. Additionally, we introduce a simple linear nonlocal model and a generalized model capable of describing arbitrary-order nonlocal effects. Finally, we examine the physical implications of these models and discuss the practical considerations necessary for implementing nonlinear nonlocal gravity. Bipartite graphs serve as a fundamental model for representing two-party systems, with numerous real-world scenarios mapped onto this framework. A specific transformation known as the vertex splitting operation is frequently employed to convert one bipartite graph into another, a process often utilized to establish equivalences between different representations of the same system. This paper introduces a straightforward FPT approach for this transformation, which involves decomposing the task into two distinct phases. The findings confirm that this method is optimal regarding the size of the parameter. Furthermore, the approach is extended to address the problem of optimizing this transformation between free products of two bipartite graphs. Ultimately, the technique is applied to reformulate a protocol for quantum key distribution over a star topology, utilizing the original product and a newly introduced tensor product of a bipartite graph. The concept of a canonical form for a bipartite graph is also defined and integrated into this optimization strategy.

This study introduces HyperDegrade, a system that prolongs the runtime of computationally intensive tasks by intentionally reducing CPU frequency, thereby extending battery life. Unlike prior methods that selectively deactivate CPU cores, HyperDegrade maintains all cores active while optimizing frequency selection. The proposed algorithm, termed HyperSlide, leverages historical workload traces to forecast future workload characteristics and dynamically adjust CPU frequency in real-time based on these predictions. Extensive evaluations using both real-world workload traces and simulated traces from the Million Instructions Per Second (MIPS) dataset demonstrate that HyperDegrade significantly enhances battery longevity compared to existing battery-saving techniques. Furthermore, the system effectively manages thermal constraints and fulfills real-time deadlines. Results indicate that HyperDegrade offers superior battery efficiency relative to previous approaches across various thermal limits and workload characteristics, with battery life improvements ranging from 1.15x to 1.27x.

The sensitivity of current gravitational-wave (GW) detectors at frequencies above 500 Hz is constrained by optical losses in recycling cavities and the fundamental shot-noise limit. To address this issue, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer (SSI) architecture, which represents a novel interferometric configuration specifically designed to enhance GW detection capabilities. By integrating an L-shaped arms configuration with the SSI design, we create a hybrid detector that combines the advantages of both approaches. This study focuses on the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer (SSI) itself, demonstrating through detailed analysis that it can significantly improve the sensitivity of conventional GW detectors at high frequencies. Furthermore, we present a practical implementation plan for this configuration within the KAGRA detector. Our findings indicate that an isolated sloshing-sagnac interferometer (SSI-I) could achieve a strain noise level of $1.4\times10^{-24}$ at 750 Hz, representing a tenfold reduction compared to the baseline L-shaped configuration of KAGRA. When implemented as a dual-recycled sloshing-sagnac interferometer (SSI-D), the strain noise level of the primary sloshing-sagnac interferometer-I can be further reduced by a factor of 1.6 at 750 Hz. These results suggest that the sloshing-sagnac interferometer offers a viable solution for boosting high-frequency sensitivity in gravitational-wave detectors. Additionally, we outline the specific requirements needed to realize this detector in the LIGO and KAGRA observatories.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for addressing spectrum scarcity in future ultra-dense networks. This paper examines the non-intersecting visibility regions among co-located APs within a non-intersecting geo-centric visible link-based XL-MIMO random access protocol. The findings indicate that these non-intersecting visibility regions among co-located APs follow a power-law distribution. Leveraging these non-intersecting regions, this work proposes an efficient protocol where the user equipment (UE) initially performs blind single-tone pilot transmission within its own visibility region, followed by an improved two-step random access procedure in the non-intersecting region managed by co-located access points. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed protocol significantly outperforms conventional protocols in terms of system throughput. Furthermore, the non-intersecting visibility regions among co-located APs can be effectively utilized to design other efficient protocols, such as connecting the UE in the non-intersecting region directly to the most suitable access point in that area, thereby enhancing system throughput. These non-intersecting regions can also be leveraged to develop effective mobility management strategies for UEs operating within those areas. Although recent advances in sequence modeling have predominantly relied on neural networks, an explicit consideration of the data-driven nature of this task suggests that neural models should be conditioned on an effective baseline. This perspective forms the foundation of our Residual Learning framework, which integrates an $n$-gram language model with a neural network to optimize text generation tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that this hybrid approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods across a range of $N$-gram and neural models on linguistic understanding tasks, including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization. Furthermore, the framework delivers significant improvements over standalone neural models in quality estimation and open-domain dialogue generation. We also provide evidence supporting the utilization of high-order $n$-gram models within this approach without increasing memory consumption. Finally, we offer additional insights into the complementary relationship between $n$-gram and neural models, as well as the benefits of incorporating higher-order $n$-grams. The proposed method is openly available at: https://github.com/Residual-LM-Group/Residual-LM.

This study introduces Informed OCR (iOCR), a framework designed to enhance the accuracy of conventional OCR systems specifically for extracting text from images of paper ballots. The goal is to support the counting of ballots identified as spoilables via image analysis. The proposed method integrates a neural network-based character identification module with a context-aware prediction module. The character identification module employs a lightweight neural network to forecast the most probable set of candidate characters for each image segment, while the context module utilizes a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to infer the correct sequence of characters based on linguistic and situational context. Experimental results demonstrate that iOCR significantly surpasses standard OCR methods in both character and word recognition rates. Furthermore, a specialized open-source toolkit has been developed to enable the application of iOCR for counting ballots flagged as spoilables through image-based detection. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1996/Informed-OCR-for-Election-Ballots.

This study examines the global atmospheric circulation patterns of Earth within a simplified two-dimensional idealized general circulation model. The model incorporates thermal and frictional forcing, along with variable topography and surface friction. Our findings indicate that circulation patterns are primarily driven by the ratio of thermal to frictional forcing and the magnitude of surface friction. Specifically, reducing the ratio of thermal to frictional forcing, or increasing surface friction, shifts the circulation from a cyclostrophic super-rotating state to a geostrophic turbulent state. In this cyclostrophic super-rotated regime, the atmosphere exhibits a single zonal jet and a series of stationary Rossby waves. Conversely, the geostrophic turbulent regime is characterized by multiple zonal jets and chaotic flow. These results offer insights into the atmospheric circulation patterns observed on terrestrial exoplanets. We introduce a reaction-diffusion formulation within the phase-space Wigner representation for the Boltzmann equation governing the dynamics of a trapped, interacting Bose gas. By employing stochastic simulations, we develop a numerical method to explore non-equilibrium dynamics and quantify the validity range of hydrodynamic descriptions. These simulations reveal that vacuum fluctuations substantially influence early-time behavior, whereas particle-pair creation becomes significant only under specific conditions. Furthermore, the simulations demonstrate that hydrodynamic models accurately describe system dynamics when collisionality is high, but fail to capture the emergence of global excitations at lower collisionalities. Finally, the study confirms that initial conditions play a critical role in determining the effectiveness of hydrodynamic approximations. The proposed reaction-diffusion approach offers a practical framework for investigating non-equilibrium dynamics using the Wigner formalism, potentially finding applications in other systems where quantum effects and non-equilibrium processes are prominent. Such investigations are particularly relevant for analyzing the early-time evolution of quantum fluids created in heavy-ion collisions.

This survey examines the Instructor-Student (IS) architecture, a family of models designed for knowledge learning. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on representation learning, the IS architecture prioritizes knowledge acquisition through an Instructor-Student (training) and Instruction-Imitation (testing) framework. Within this framework, the Instructor performs a specific task, such as answering a question, while the Student learns from the demonstration. During testing, the Student executes the task independently. The core objective of this architecture is to construct a knowledge base (KB) that enables the Student to perform tasks autonomously. The IS architecture comprises three primary variants: the Direct Feedback IS (DF-IS), Indirect Feedback IS (ID-IS), and Meta-Learning IS (ML-IS). These variants differ based on how the Student model is trained and how the knowledge base is constructed. We provide a comprehensive overview of the DF-IS, ID-IS, and ML-IS architectures, detailing their knowledge base construction methods, training strategies, and applications. Furthermore, we identify current limitations and propose potential future research directions. The table of contents is as follows: Section 2 introduces the concept of Knowledge Learning (KL); Section 3 provides a high-level description of the IS architecture; Section 4 details the construction of knowledge bases for various IS architectures; Section 5 analyzes the three primary IS architectures; Section 6 categorizes applications of IS architectures for knowledge learning; Section 7 discusses existing limitations and potential future research avenues; and finally, Section 8 offers our conclusions. The necessary mathematical notations are defined in Appendix A.

This study addresses the bias affecting the $B_{\rm LOS}$ histogram in data generated by inversion codes applied to synthetic datasets created by forward models. Applied to a solar event analyzed using the AsOfInv global inversion code, the correction reveals that previous conclusions regarding the emergence of a flux rope were influenced by this bias. For any finite classical group $G$ acting on a vector space $V$, we define and examine the lattice $\mathcal{B}(V)$ consisting of the boolean subgroups generated by invertible diagonal matrices. Our findings demonstrate that this lattice is atomic, distributive, and graded, with its rank corresponding to the product of the dimensions of $V$ and the order of $G$ divided by $|GL_2(\mathbb{F})|$, where $\mathbb{F}$ represents the underlying field. Additionally, we characterize the atoms and elements of rank two within this lattice. These characteristics are utilized to provide a complete description of boolean subgroups of $G$ that are isomorphic to $B_3$, $A_4$, $S_3\times S_2$, $D_8$, $C_3\times C_2$, $C_4\times C_2$, and $C_2\times C_2\times C_2$. Furthermore, we establish that the lattice $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is IS-limited if and only if the product of $|G|$ and the dimension of $V$ does not exceed six, a result that yields a novel proof of a theorem by Aschenbrenner, Baker, and Mildenberger regarding the IS-limited nature of $G$'s inversion subgroups. The completeness of the lattice of boolean diagonal subgroups also offers a fresh characterization of classical groups via their root systems. Furthermore, for the symplectic group $Sp_{2n}(q)$, we identify the maximal subgroup that is not a boolean diagonal subgroup, a discovery with significant implications for the study of maximal subgroups of classical groups. These results contribute to the understanding of invertible subgroups defined by specific matrices, particularly sparse ones, across various areas of group theory.

Finally, we explore the notion of timelike curves in semi-metric spaces that possess two distinct timelike Bertrand curves. This study addresses the classification of cardiac audio under conditions of additive noise and convolutional distortion. By leveraging a dataset of heart sounds collected from a real-world environment, we observe that the network's decision boundaries shift when additive noise is introduced post-filtration. To tackle this challenge, we propose a framework for heart sound categorization that jointly manages both distortion types. The approach involves a two-stage pipeline: first, an initial classifier separates cardiac audio into clean and noisy segments, with the latter further divided into three groups based on noise intensity; second, a specialized network processes each segment group to predict the correct phonosegment label. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this method surpasses existing techniques, achieving an accuracy of 97.01%. Additionally, the proposed framework exhibits robustness against higher levels of noise and convolutional distortion. Open source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/HeartSoundCategorization.

This study examines the interconnection between the molecular mass ($\rm M_{CO}$) and the mass of atomic hydrogen ($\rm M_{HI}$) in a extensive collection of star-forming galaxies, with the goal of investigating the underexcitation of C\,I line emission relative to CO emission within the associated molecular gas reservoirs. Initially, we outline the characteristics of the $\rm M_{HI} - M_{CO}$ scatter and its variations across different mass ranges. We then present a detailed analysis of the excitation conditions, utilizing a simple model to derive the "effective" temperatures ($T_{\rm eff}$) of the CI ladders and the CO ladder. Our results indicate that the scatter in the $\rm M_{HI} - M_{CO}$ relation correlates with the degree of CI underexcitation alongside the number of CO transitions employed for CO ladder modeling. Furthermore, we find that the underexcitation of the CI lines is most likely a subthermal effect, occurring because the gas densities are too low to fully excite the CI ladders, rather than a consequence of low temperatures. We conclude by exploring the potential utility of leveraging the underexcitation of specific CI lines—particularly the $j=3\rightarrow2$ and $j=4\rightarrow3$ transitions—in conjunction with CO lines to constrain CO ladder models and thereby refine the estimation of $\rm M_{CO}$ and $\rm M_{HI}$. Such an approach could help reduce uncertainties in molecular and atomic mass measurements by approximately a factor of two, which is particularly advantageous for investigations involving the total gas mass, surface density, and star formation efficiency. Additionally, the $\rm M_{HI} - M_{CO}$ data can serve as a valuable consistency check for proposed models describing the coexistence of HI and CO, such as the segregation model and the bimodal model. We also briefly address the significance of the underexcitation of CI lines relative to CO lines in the context of future JWST observations of the molecular gas reservoirs of high-redshift galaxies. We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions, the evolution of particle velocities along the line is a non-simple diffusion with state-dependent reflection boundaries. Leveraging this finding, we establish limit theorems for the velocity process along nearly linear trajectories. These results generalize prior work by Angel, Coletti, and co-authors, which applied only to asymmetric simple exclusion processes. Furthermore, we derive limit theorems for particle positions along linear paths and confirm that fluctuations follow a Tracy-Widom distribution on the macroscopic limit. These conclusions hold for any initial gradient profile of particle currents. Finally, we extend these results to initial conditions with a shock, showing that the process converges to a mixture of the limiting distributions associated with the left and right initial states. These outcomes provide a comprehensive description of ASEP fluctuations across all possible initial conditions. Ultimately, these limit theorems serve as a foundational tool for analyzing other stochastic processes constructed from ASEP, particularly in the context of last passage percolation on last-particle processes. Mathematical models of disease transmission are essential for evaluating control strategies and offering guidance during epidemics. In the current SARS-CoV-2 outbreak, a wide array of models has been developed, yet there is no single ideal model that encompasses all necessary aspects. Selecting the most suitable model for specific scenarios remains a significant challenge. This paper provides a review of various models used to address different problems related to the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. We begin by outlining the fundamental components of epidemic models and their primary objectives. Subsequently, we examine specific models designed for distinct issues, ranging from estimating key parameters like the basic reproduction number and generation time, to assessing the efficacy of interventions and exploring potential transmission mechanisms. Finally, we discuss the future directions required to enhance our understanding of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and other viral outbreaks. The accompanying figure illustrates the diverse range of problems tackled by different models during the current crisis. This article serves as a comprehensive overview, complementing existing review literature on epidemic modeling (for instance, [1–3]) by specifically focusing on the problems solved by various models rather than providing detailed mathematical formulations. As a companion to our earlier work [4], which analyzed the reliability of epidemiological indicators in the present epidemic, this paper also addresses the estimation of fundamental parameters such as the basic reproduction number, effective reproduction number, and generation time. That previous work emphasized the importance of these parameters and their estimation methods for understanding and managing epidemic spread. In the current situation, numerous estimates for these parameters have been published; however, many lack sufficient methodological detail to be fully reproducible. Furthermore, there is a risk of misinterpreting these estimates if the underlying assumptions and methods are not clearly understood. For example, comparing the "R values" of two regions with different control measures is meaningless unless those measures are also taken into account. Similarly, an "R value" of 1 offers no insight into the appropriate level of intervention required, as it provides no information regarding the speed of epidemic growth or decline. While these parameters are useful for monitoring the impact of interventions, they are insufficient for determining the most effective control strategies. In this context, direct simulation of transmission dynamics is necessary to evaluate the efficacy of specific interventions. Throughout this review, we use the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic as a concrete example to illustrate the strengths and limitations of different modeling approaches for various challenges. To address this, we integrated a simple model of nuclear star formation with the M*-SFR model by Buitrago et al. (2012) to replicate the observational data. Furthermore, the model successfully reproduces the central sf rate saturation above 10\,10\,9\,M\* without requiring a global sf rate drop-off at a specific level. Consequently, our findings suggest that the flattening of the log(M\*)-log(sfr) slope at massive log(M\*) > 10\,10\,9\,M\* is caused by a central structural evolution, manifested as a shrinking nuclear radius, rather than a decline in efficiency. Rapidly rotating low-mass stars, known as Gamma Doradus variables, were recently identified in the Hyades cluster. These stars exhibit rotation periods roughly half as long as those of the standard low-mass gamma oscillation pulsators found in the same cluster. Given that the angular rotation rates of low-mass stars are constrained by viscous and gravitational torques, the Gamma Doradus variable's period is likely too short for its spin rate to be achieved through standard angular momentum accumulation. Consequently, an additional mechanism must have accelerated this star. We examine two potential solutions: the accretion and destruction of a low-mass planet, and an anomalous enhancement of angular momentum transport. By constructing a detailed evolutionary track for a 0.9 solar mass star in the Hyades, we demonstrate that consuming a planet with a mass of 0.01 solar ones requires an efficient transport of angular momentum via a viscous torque corresponding to an alpha value of approximately 0.003. This efficiency aligns with that observed during the early phases of stellar evolution. Furthermore, if the destruction of a more massive planet (0.02 solar masses) occurred at a faster rotation rate, the resulting spin would match the Gamma Doradus variable's period, implying an alpha value of approximately 0.006. Ultimately, determining whether a specific Gamma Doradus variable star was spun up by planet destruction or by a heightened viscous torque remains challenging without a more precise understanding of the low-mass star's angular momentum history. This review also highlights the significant implications of the Gamma Doradus variable's discovery for the study of low-mass stellar rotation. The accompanying figure illustrates how the spin rate of a 0.9 solar mass star is limited by viscous and gravitational torques as a function of rotation period. It depicts the torque dominance regions, the maximum rotation rate feasible for a 0.9 solar mass star in the Hyades via angular momentum accumulation (dashed line), and the period of the Gamma Doradus variable (solid line). The figure also outlines the parameters necessary to spin up the Gamma Doradus variable by destroying a 0.01 solar mass planet and the efficiency of viscous torque required to achieve the same result through anomalous angular momentum transport.

Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, posing significant dangers by misleading the public and exacerbating societal divisions. While existing detection methods perform well on labeled datasets, they fail to generalize when test data lacks labels. Furthermore, current approaches rely heavily on manual feature engineering, which is difficult to scale. In contrast, deep learning-based solutions offer a more automated alternative. This study introduces MetaFEND, a framework that utilizes meta-learning to enable generalization from few-shot samples and fosters cross-domain transfer learning. Specifically, we apply a neural process network to learn detection models for verified news, which then serve as a source domain to support detection in unverified content through meta-learning. To handle the multimodal characteristics of news articles, we incorporate a lightweight encoder-based module. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework effectively generalizes to unseen datasets and outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the MetaFEND model successfully identifies false news samples within completely new datasets, as illustrated in Figure 1. Given the escalating volume of misinformation, this work provides an automated solution for detecting fake news in datasets where human annotation is either costly or impractical. The proposed MetaFEND framework is open-source and accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Multimodal_Emergent False_News_Detection_Via_Meta Neural_Process_Networks. Our findings indicate that meta-learning effectively enables generalization to unseen datasets and successfully detects false news in completely new data, including the creation of a dataset for Indian news in collaboration with the Times Group.

Utilizing this decomposition, we develop designs for GCMs of bi-quaternary and bi-octavianary orders, as well as their corresponding GCAs of bi-quaternary and bi-octavianary polyphase types. Synthetic data serves as a crucial resource for training deep learning models when real-world data is scarce, potentially enhancing the care of specific patient populations. Despite its advantages, generating medical data remains challenging due to the difficulty of preserving semantic information, a requirement particularly vital for clinical applications. This paper introduces a novel framework for brain injury synthesis built upon a progressive brain injury variational auto-encoder (P-Brivae) that integrates a variational approach with two adversarial networks. Initially, an image-to-image (I2I) generative adversarial network (GAN) converts healthy brain images into latent representations, which are then processed by the Brivae to reconstruct images of brain injuries. Finally, a second I2I GAN refines these outputs to improve realism. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current brain injury synthesis techniques in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Furthermore, the framework's utility is validated through a classification task utilizing an independent real brain injury dataset. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Brain-Imagelab/PAVE-Brain.

This paper introduces a unified framework for feature extraction using contrastive learning, addressing both self-supervised and semi-supervised learning scenarios. The proposed framework consists of two primary components: a negative sampling module and a contrastive module. Crucially, these components operate independently of one another. To enhance the contrastive module, we introduce a novel module termed the "similarity module," which functions as a supplementary component alongside the negative sampling module within the overall architecture. Extensive experiments conducted across four datasets confirm that this framework outperforms current state-of-the methods in both self-supervised and semi-supervised contexts. Furthermore, the study provides detailed analyses of the similarities and contrasts between the feature vectors generated by the similarity module and those produced by the negative sampling module when used individually as the contrastive component. These findings offer valuable insights for future research in this domain. Ultimately, this work presents a comprehensive, unified structure for feature extraction based on contrastive learning, applicable to various tasks including classification, retrieval, and graph node representation. The approach relies on a triad of modules: the contrastive module, the negative sampling module, and the similarity module. By combining any two of these modules as the source of positive and negative samples for the contrastive module, one can derive three distinct feature extraction strategies: contrastive learning with Euclidean distance, self-supervised contrastive learning, and a new method called similarity-based feature extraction. These strategies were validated on four datasets, with results demonstrating that the framework surpasses existing solutions. The paper concludes with a call for further research to develop additional methods by integrating all three modules. Key contributions include the introduction of the similarity module, the establishment of a unified framework for feature extraction via contrastive learning, and the derivation and testing of three specific methods within this framework. Although large language models (LLMs) excel at numerous tasks, their integration into real-world applications remains constrained by the difficulty of verifying generated outputs and the challenge of incorporating domain-specific knowledge. This study introduces a lightweight method for injecting structured knowledge into LLMs to enhance the accuracy of text generation. We introduce a novel framework that converts knowledge graphs into a latent textual representation, enabling the model to process this knowledge without direct access to the graph itself. We open-sourced the corresponding Python library at https://github.com/AsafYehudai/LLM-SKILL. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly boosts the factual correctness of outputs from state-of-the-art open-source LLMs across multiple downstream applications. Furthermore, our method improves factual accuracy by up to 10.1 percentage points compared to previous knowledge-based techniques for improving semantic textual similarity. Finally, the framework delivers a 15% gain in factual correctness over a baseline utilizing an external large language model. These results confirm that our technique effectively augments the correctness of knowledge graph-based methods, validating its utility for enhancingLLMs through the introduction of additional structured knowledge. Ultimately, SKILL offers a lightweight, effective solution for improving the factual accuracy of both LLMs and other natural language processing systems via the incorporation of structured knowledge. To our knowledge, this work represents the initial attempt to convert a knowledge graph into a latent textual form for use by LLMs, thereby increasing the capacity of these models to ingest and leverage such knowledge. We anticipate that this technique will find widespread application in improving the factual correctness of language tasks, including machine translation, textual entailment, and more. Our framework consists of three primary components: (1) a graph-to-text module that generates latent representations of knowledge graphs, (2) a knowledge-aware tokenizer capable of encoding these representations, and (3) a knowledge graph encoder responsible for creating embeddings for these representations to support downstream reasoning. This study examines these concepts using the tomograms of Gaussian states for systems comprising one or two harmonic oscillators. The findings demonstrate that within the tomographic framework, entanglement appears as a loss of concavity, whereas synchronization is revealed through the emergence of dual-peaked structures. These results offer a straightforward method for identifying both phenomena in non-negative function representations, such as probability and quasiprobability distributions. Furthermore, the results indicate that the transition between single-peaked and dual-peaked structures in non-negative functions during synchronization is a global effect, whereas manifestations of entanglement in these same functions are local in nature. Ultimately, this work provides evidence that detecting non-classical phenomena in non-negative functions requires analyzing global characteristics, similar to the approach used for wave functions. We present an algorithm to construct the submodule lattice of a multiplicity-free module from its character. This construction utilizes a lattice derived from the collection of maximal submodules, which is achieved through an integration of the Birkhoff theorem and the Amalgamation theorem for distributive lattices. Consequently, the initial step involves determining all maximal submodules, a task for which we have also developed an algorithm. The algorithms for constructing both the distributive lattice of characteristic functions and the submodule lattice have been implemented in Sage. Furthermore, the algorithm designed to identify all maximal submodules has been incorporated into the same software as a standard function. Our constructed submodule lattice serves as a comprehensive overview of the module's structure, offering a more extensive perspective than the composition series. This detailed structure facilitates the identification of specific submodules of interest, such as those with simple or multiplicity one multiplicities. Additionally, the lattice of all submodules with a given multiplicity $k$ constitutes a graded poset, which can be employed to investigate the multiplicities of its elements. As an application, we define a function on the set of submodule multiples of multiplicity one, termed the Euler function, and explore its properties. We have also formulated a conjecture regarding the Euler function and its connection to the collection of submodule multiples of multiplicity one. Finally, we have implemented an algorithm to calculate the multiplicity of any specific submodule within the lattice. Key terms: submodule lattice, multiplicity, multiplicity free, Amalgamation theorem, Birkhoff theorem, multipole, Euler function, multipole polynomial, multipole tree, multiplicity poset, Sage. This study examines biharmonic hypersurfaces equipped with recurrent second fundamental tensors, Ricci tensors, or related structures within Euclidean space. It establishes that such hypersurfaces must be trivial. Furthermore, the research investigates biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space possessing recurrent mechanisms, specifically those with recurrent harmonic second fundamental tensors. The work also explores whether biharmonic hypersurfaces with recurrent first or second mean curvature vectors exist in Euclidean space, concluding with a summary of the key findings regarding these areas. Automated testing serves as a vital technique for enhancing the reliability of software systems. This paper introduces a geometric method for unit testing that facilitates the systematic coverage of all combinations of boundary conditions and deeper nesting levels within variables. Unlike traditional approaches, this geometric technique does not require a predefined ranking of variables to guide coverage. The method employs a specialized algorithm to identify optimal test sets for covering variable conditions, leveraging a visual representation of the program's execution path on a grid. This grid is constructed by plotting the ranges of two target variables on the X and Y axes, with each program statement mapped to a specific coordinate. By analyzing this grid, the algorithm selects the most effective combination of test cases to satisfy coverage goals. The proposed approach is applicable to various coverage criteria, with a specific focus on All Boundary Conditions (ABC) and All Conditions (AC). Empirical results demonstrate that this geometric method aligns with conventional techniques for achieving boundary and all-condition coverage. Furthermore, the algorithm successfully identifies minimal test sets for two boundary-related criteria (ABC and RABC) and two all-related criteria (AC and RAC) across 19 KCR knowledge base functions, yielding improvements of 17%, 20%, 13%, and 13% respectively compared to existing methods. For the Apache JPEGBenchmark and ExpressBenchmark benchmarks, the results from this geometric approach matched those of a leading state-of-the-art tool, confirming its efficacy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a minimal test set was derived for the All Conditions (AC) criterion using a purely automatic method. Additionally, the algorithm can support other coverage criteria, such as Restricted All Zero One (RAZO) and RAZO+, by extending the coverage grid to include additional rows and columns. Beyond testing, this technique can benefit other fields, including formal verification, where it can aid in constructing execution traces for specific inputs to validate properties, and in education, where it can assist in generating examples for curriculum materials. Fiber-reinforced composites featuring an embedded sensor network have the potential to detect and localize damage through changes in electrical conductivity. However, repairing such damage remains challenging, particularly when the material is used in critical applications like aerospace. This study introduces a genetic algorithm-based electrical impedance tomography technique to reconstruct damage images in self-sensing unidirectional glass fiber-reinforced polymer (UD-GFEP) composites, aiming for precise reconstruction in areas previously deemed difficult. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that these composites can achieve exact damage shaping during repair via a drilling and adhesive-based process. Experimental results indicate that the electrical impedance tomography reconstruction via the genetic algorithm offers superior accuracy compared to conventional methods, such as backprojection, for reconstructing complex cracks. Additionally, the damage shaping is executed with high precision, maintaining an error margin of less than 1.5 mm. These findings confirm that the proposed combination of electrical impedance tomography and damage shaping effectively addresses both under-construction detection and reconstruction problems in self-sensing UD-GFEP composites. Ultimately, this approach could enable a shift from open-loop to closed-loop damage control in such materials. We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean space that employs a specific set of geometric entities as fundamental components. This approach enables the construction of equivalent descriptions utilizing these geometric elements, which in turn facilitates the derivation of identity relations connecting them. The detailed development of this tensor formalism and the exploration of applications based on this concept are presented throughout the paper. These concepts find utility in Euclidean spaces and, with suitable modifications, in complex spaces, particularly when addressing problems involving the rotation group and its related groups. The introduction of this formalism into physics has the potential to yield new identity relations among geometric elements, potentially serving as valuable tools for solving physics problems. Furthermore, this framework could aid in the development of a theory of geometry from the perspective of fundamental physics, where geometric entities are treated as fundamental concepts rather than tensor components. Such an initiative might offer fresh insights into the unification of physics with the theory of gravity. We also examine this formalism within complex spaces, deriving specific elements of interest for applications related to the groups $U(3)$, $SU(3)$, and their extensions.

This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm for matrix inversion, expanding the range of orders applicable to a specific class of positive semi-definite matrices. The proposed method achieves an asymptotic computational complexity of $O(n^2/\log(n))$ per iteration, where $n$ represents the matrix dimension. When integrated with a fast linear operator—such as the Newton iteration or a recursive convolution-based approach—on graphic processing units (GPUs), this technique surpasses conventional inversion methods for matrices of specific sizes. It is particularly advantageous in scenarios involving repeatedly updated matrices, for instance, within adaptive filtering applications. The algorithm's general form is: $A_{k+1} = A_0 - (I - (A_0 H_n)^{2^k}) A_0 ((A_0 H_n)^{2^k} A_0)^T$, with $H_n$ denoting a linear operator tailored to the dimension $n$. Empirical evidence from 2D radar sensor data indicates that combining the third-order method with the Newton iteration offers the best performance for the data analyzed in this paper. Furthermore, utilizing the reciprocal Newton iteration yields superior results when the initial guess matrix is the identity.

We conducted global 3D hydrodynamic simulations to examine how dust evolution influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. Our findings indicate that while gas cooling drives VSI growth in simulations with constant dust opacity, the optical depth generated by dust settling ultimately suppresses this instability. In models featuring a power-law opacity, dust accumulation in the midplane reduces the frequency-dependent background cooling timescale, initially accelerating VSI growth; however, the resulting midplane opacity still inhibits the instability. Furthermore, dust settling diminishes vertical turbulence, causing gas to settle further and amplifying midplane opacity, which ultimately curtails VSI development. These results suggest that dust evolution plays a critical role in regulating the vertical instability in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Consequently, the settling of both gas and dust may have enabled the emergence of global radial instabilities, such as the gravitational instability, in the early phases of disk evolution. Our conclusions rely on a simple dust opacity model and may require revision if future observations reveal a more complex opacity behavior than anticipated. Global 3D simulations incorporating realistic dust oponomies derived from radiative transfer calculations based on actual dust properties are necessary to fully understand the interplay between dust evolution and global instabilities during the early evolution of protoplanetary disks. Such investigations could offer insights into the formation mechanisms of giant planets. Additionally, our results imply that the lack of observed global instabilities in the outer regions of mature disks can be attributed to dust evolution, thereby contradicting the predictions of local instability models that assume constant opacity. Ultimately, dust evolution serves as a crucial factor in the transition from planet formation in the outer regions of primordial disks to the migration and accretion of giant planets onto their host stars in mature systems. This mechanism helps explain how giant planets form in the outer zones of early disks and migrate inward in the later stages of a planet disk's lifecycle. Regarding the inner regions, our simulations demonstrate that dust settling does not significantly alter the dominance of spiral arm-driven instabilities, such as the VSI or gravitational instability, in driving turbulence. Therefore, future research should focus on the inner regions to uncover mechanisms responsible for creating the calm environments required for the formation of super-Earths and Earth-like planets. This paper addresses the issue of dynamic backdoors in deep neural networks (DNNs), where a malicious actor adds a backdoor to a model without direct access. Such attacks are particularly concerning because they are difficult to detect and can introduce covert functionalities into models that appear benign. Existing solutions typically involve poisoning images during training with a global mean pooling (GMP) layer, which simplifies the recognition of poisoned inputs. However, this approach limits the design of trigger patterns and often results in ineffective triggers. Furthermore, it is unclear whether a GMP-free dynamic backdoor is feasible. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate that a GMP-free dynamic backdoor is indeed possible. Specifically, we propose a method to construct a complex trigger shape—a teddy bear—on an image and guide the model to misclassify it as a specified target. Additionally, we introduce a technique to create a visible trigger that remains undetectable by standard anomaly-based detection methods. Our constructed triggers are more complex and stealthier than previous designs. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the trigger's complexity, stealthiness, and generalizability across various architectures and datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenyuxiang/DynamicBackdoorWithGBMP.

This paper introduces a new regularization strategy that leverages the AWKWARD framework \cite{aguiar2022an} to generate predictions from a teacher network in a structured manner. Genuine nonlocal phenomena, such as Bell nonlocality and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering, typically manifest through the nonlocal character of composite quantum systems. This paper demonstrates that the nonlocality of a system's single-particle state—specifically single-particle entanglement—can produce genuinely nonlocal effects, including the single-particle form of EPR steering. We establish that single-particle entanglement enables the occurrence of single-particle Bell nonlocality and EPR steering, which collectively account for all nine distinct genuine nonlocal effects. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric for quantifying single-particle entanglement and prove the inequality $\mathcal{M} \ge \mathcal{N}$, where $\mathcal{M}$ represents the measure of nonlocality and $\mathcal{N}$ denotes the measure of single-particle entanglement. As a direct application of this result, we show that optimizing the nonlocality of the N00N state yields the highest possible single-particle entanglement. Complementarily, we derive the optimal strategies for demonstrating both single-particle Bell nonlocality and EPR steering. Finally, we confirm that the single-particle entanglement of the Fock state $|n\rangle$ equals $n$, implying that the nonlocality of its N00N superpositions is limited by this same Fock state number $n$. These findings collectively reveal that single-particle entanglement gives rise to all nine genuine nonlocal effects, a phenomenon we term "single-particle nonlocality." Consequently, this work underscores the significant role of nonlocality in quantum resource theories. Additionally, the proposed framework offers a practical method for enhancing the nonlocality of single-particle states, which can be directly applied to improve the precision of measurement-based quantum metrology. The concepts and techniques developed here are also expected to prove valuable for addressing similar challenges in other quantum information science domains. This manuscript is intended for the collection of papers titled: Nonlocality, Steering and Entanglement: New Developments and Applications.

This paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design framework for energy-efficient lstms. Initially, we present a low-rank hierarchical tensor decomposition (LHTD) approach to compress LSTM weights, followed by a hardware-friendly lhtd-LSTM network architecture. Subsequently, we designed a high-performance, energy-efficient LHTD-LSTM ASIC, validating the efficacy of our algorithm and hardware co-design for LHTD-LSTM networks. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that an  lhtd-LSTM  with  90\%  accuracy  requires  3.77×  fewer  parameters  and  4.01×  less  area  than  a  standard  LSTM  to  achieve  the  same  level  of  performance.  Furthermore,  the  proposed  lhtd-LSTM  achieves  17.71×  higher  performance  per  watt  compared  to  the  conventional  LSTM.  The  described  algorithm  and  hardware  co-design  framework  for  weight  low-rank  hierarchical  tensor  decomposition  offers  significant  advantages  in  parameter  count,  area,  and  performance  per  watt  without  compromising  accuracy,  making  it  particularly  beneficial  for  deploying  lhtd-LSTM  networks  on  resource-constrained  devices  for  video  identification  and  related  applications.  To  the  best  of  our  knowledge,  this  represents  the  first  report  on  the  co-design  of  an  LSTM  processing  unit  and  a  low  rank  hierarchical  tensor  decomposition  unit  specifically  for  video  identification.  The  proposed  algorithm  and  hardware  co-design  framework  for  LHTD  can  also  be  applied  to  other  neural  network  topologies  facing  similar  challenges  in  resource-constrained  environments. This study examines the Schr\"odinger equation defined on the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle within $\R^2$ or $\R^3$, which contains the origin. The boundary conditions alternate between Dirichlet and Neumann, while initial data satisfies a combination of subcritical mass and focally negative energy. Under these circumstances, it is demonstrated that the solution experiences finite-time blowup. The findings extend upon the work of Merle, Rodnianski, and Sterbenz \cite{MRS} for the free Schr\"odinger equation on $\R^2$ and $\R^3$, as well as the research of the current authors \cite{BDM} for the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation inside a convex domain. A crucial element of this proof involves establishing a local smoothing effect in the exterior of a convex obstacle, detailed in this paper. Furthermore, the authors derive a global uniform bound for the solution within a specific anisotropic Sobolev space, leveraging a recent result by the first author \cite{B} on the Schr\"odinger equation on $\R^2$. These conclusions are achieved by utilizing a concentration function and a corresponding energy concentration function, alongside a novel local dispersion estimate valid in the exterior of a convex obstacle. Notably, the proof of this new local smoothing effect relies on a recent global smoothing result by the first two authors \cite{BD} for Schr\"odinger equations associated with metric perturbations of hyperbolic space. Finally, the authors also present a blowup alternative tailored to this setting.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of scientific inquiry, yet selecting an appropriate testing method for specific research questions remains challenging. While p-values have long been utilized for this purpose, recent years have seen a surge in interest toward alternative approaches, most notably Bayes factors. Despite this growing focus, the application of Bayes factors has been hindered by significant criticisms regarding their sensitivity to prior choices, a problem often compounded by the use of inappropriate prior specifications. This manuscript revisits these concerns and demonstrates that recent advancements in objective prior methods, combined with hybrid strategies incorporating p-value testing, can effectively address these issues. Furthermore, we clarify common misunderstandings concerning the suitability of default priors for likelihood-based model comparison and provide practical guidelines for implementing these solutions. Ultimately, this work offers a set of actionable recommendations for researchers aiming to employ Bayes factors, whether as a standalone approach or alongside other hypothesis testing methods. These strategies are detailed through concrete examples involving the analysis of gravitational wave data. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/robertgagnier/RobustBayesFactor.

This study introduces DiscSense, a system designed to evaluate the performance of classifiers tasked with identifying and classifying discourse markers. Unlike previous evaluations that primarily focused on whether a linking expression between two sentences received the correct label, DiscSense offers a granular, automated assessment of both detection and classification across various linguistic categories. The outcome of this examination serves as a metric for the combination of precision and recall, referred to as the "sensescore." We applied this framework to three state-of-the-art systems operating on two discourse classification tasks: the challenge dataset and a larger, unlabeled collection known as Facebook. The analysis reveals that no system achieves high accuracy for all categories within either dataset. Furthermore, the findings indicate that category definitions require refinement, as numerous instances are being classified into incorrect categories. For the Facebook dataset, the results also suggest that the volume of examples per category is insufficient to train effective neural networks. Ultimately, this granular analysis provides valuable insights for enhancing both the discourse marker classification tasks and the specific systems evaluated. To support this goal, we will release the accompanying Python code and the "sensescore" metric as open-source resources.

This paper introduces a unified family of twists derived from the Jordanian $r$-matrix, which acts upon the tensor product of the universal enveloping algebra of a Borel subalgebra and its dual. These twists facilitate the deformation of both the (negative) Borel subalgebra and its enveloping algebra. Furthermore, the study involves the connection between this family and the standard Drinfeld twist, as well as with the canonical twist associated with the opposite Borel subalgebra. Finally, the work examines how this family of Jordanian twists interacts with the Drinfeld double of a Borel subalgebra's universal enveloping algebra. This investigation extends a similar analysis conducted by the authors regarding Lie group twists and their counterparts in the enveloping algebra of a semisimple Lie algebra. The results demonstrate that the Jordanian twist modifies the coproduct, deforms the classical $r$-matrix, and leaves the universal $R$-matrix unchanged. Conversely, as a Lie group Lie algebra twist, it does not alter the universal Lie algebra $r$-matrix but induces changes in the coproduct and the classical $r$-matrix. These findings highlight that the universal Lie algebra $r$-matrix serves as the fundamental invariant under the action of Lie group Lie algebra twists. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the previously defined negative Drinfeld-Jordanian twist is actually a combination of the standard positive Drinfeld twist and a conventional Lie group Lie algebra twist. This work was motivated by the pursuit of a twist operator capable of regularizing the regularization-independent "true" universal $R$-matrix, a concept explored in the authors' earlier research. Ultimately, such an operator will enable the definition of a deformed (negative) Borel subalgebra that is dual to the family of deformed (negative) universal enveloping algebras via a universal intertwining operator, effectively functioning as a "true" Jordanian K\"{a}hler differential. Such a differential will be useful for constructing star-products on the corresponding universal enveloping algebra. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for the exact solution of constraints involving union, concatenation, and a new class of star operators termed "extended stars," which generalize both iteration and power operators. The proposed algorithm operates without relying on iterative methods, enabling it to address highly iterative expressions efficiently. Additionally, the algorithm determines equivalence between two extended regular expressions and verifies the emptiness of an individual extended regular expression. These capabilities are applicable to areas such as access control systems, protocol specification, and compilation. The algorithm is described as a combination of four components: a top-down symbolic term rewriting system, a bottom-up symbolic gathering mechanism, a finite automaton construction procedure, and an exactness verification method. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing approaches in terms of efficiency. The source code and further details are accessible at https://github.com/chenyong01/SymbolicSolvingOfExtendedRegularExpressionConstraints.

This study examines the spinning OPE block associated with a primary operator inserted at infinity within the vacuum CFT_2 defined on the upper half plane (UHP). By utilizing image operator techniques, we demonstrate that the block under consideration can be expressed as a superposition of conventional primary blocks and a series involving spinning conformal blocks of dual primary operators. These dual primaries reside on the boundary line (y=0) of the UHP and correspond to the product of the original primary with its image. Leveraging the orthogonality of conformal blocks, we establish that this expansion constitutes a complete decomposition. Furthermore, we validate these findings numerically for specific low-lying spinning OPE blocks. We also explore the implications of this decomposition for the bootstrap approach, particularly regarding the construction of spinning OPE blocks. Finally, we address the feasibility of defining such blocks for primary operators whose conformal dimensions are not fixed, and whose spins are either continuous or restricted to even integers. In the context of the bootstrap, we derive a linear equation governing the decomposition of spinning OPE blocks into four-point conformal blocks, and we formulate a method to extract the coefficients of dual spinning blocks from this relation. We conclude by highlighting the challenges in applying this method to theories with a finite spectrum of conformal blocks. Regarding the operator product block, we propose an alternative strategy for introducing spinning OPE blocks into the bootstrap framework. As an application, we analyze the bootstrap equation for theories defined on the UHP and derive a simplified linear equation for the coefficient of a dual spinning conformal block, achieved by combining the standard bootstrap equation with the aforementioned linear relation for OPE blocks. We also investigate the feasibility of solving this equation numerically. In the course of this analysis, we identify a significant issue with the conventional implementation of the conformal block equation on the UHP. Additionally, we consider the utility of the recently developed differential equation method for CFT_1 bootstrap problems in addressing this challenge within the CFT_2 bootstrap. We close by outlining a potential solution to this difficulty. Throughout this work, we adopt the convention that the product of two primary operators with helicities h_1 and h_2 carries a helicity equal to the difference between their conformal spins, i.e., h_1 - h_2.

This study introduces a novel architecture for lobster-eye X-ray optics, enabling the creation of wide-field monitors with unprecedented coverage. The implementation involves multiplexing multiple segments of a curved lobster-eye structure. We conducted laboratory experiments using a 20° x 20° field of view (FoV) to validate the concept with three segments, achieving a total FoV of 60° x 20°. These trials confirmed that the multiplexed configuration preserves image quality and that the source positions remain accurately determined across the combined field. Additionally, the design maintains a constant focal length for all segments, ensuring that images from each section are precisely aligned at the focal plane. Given that a lobster-eye optic offers omnidirectional imaging, a system comprising just 12 segments could monitor a sky area of 200,000 square degrees with a 60° x 20° FoV. Such a wide-field monitoring capability is particularly valuable for identifying transient events, which can be followed up by imaging telescopes with higher spatial resolution. Furthermore, this architecture could serve as an effective solution for the large-field imaging requirements of future X-ray missions. The concept of multiplexing curved lobster-eye optics is applicable to fields beyond astrophysics, including solar physics and various industrial sectors.

This study employs machine learning to examine how the causal cosmic velocity field influences the dark matter halo mass function. By training a neural network on a dark matter-only simulation, we derived halo abundance predictions across a range of densities and masses from both standard and anisotropic modified gravity models. These forecasts were then compared against results from the UNRAVELLED framework, which utilizes the causal velocity field to determine halo formation. Our analysis confirms that the dark matter halo mass function derived from the causal speed field aligns closely with the outcome obtained using the anisotropic modified gravity models. Furthermore, we find that incorporating the causal velocity field into the UNRAVELLED framework yields a more significant modification of the halo mass function than the anisotropic modified gravity models. These results indicate that the UNRAVELLED model is more effective at enhancing light halo suppression through the causal velocity field than the anisotropic modified gravity models, suggesting that the latter may lack sufficient strength to fully account for halo suppression via the velocity field. Consequently, the remaining suppression must be addressed by other mechanisms, such as the expansion of the Hubble flow. We conclude by proposing future research directions. Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge. In this study, we demonstrate that an atom interferometer can identify extremely weak magnetic fields by leveraging the Meissner effect to amplify the response of atoms to local field changes. This method relies on the spatial separation of atomic wave packets, which traverse regions with distinct magnetic characteristics. By employing a superconducting slab, we successfully detected local field variations as small as 0.3 nT. Furthermore, we theoretically establish that this approach could achieve a sensitivity of 0.03 pT over an integration period of one hour. This sensitivity is comparable to the best existing sensors operating in the same frequency range, yet it is attained using a straightforward configuration. The potential applications of this technique extend to geophysical surveys, archaeological investigations, and the detection of magnetic anomalies caused by concealed objects. Additionally, this method offers a practical means to test for hidden superconducting materials, for instance, to verify the authenticity of historical artifacts. The proposed sensor consists of a simple arrangement of two atom interferometers and a single superconducting slab, making it a viable candidate for future deployment. Detailed descriptions of the experimental setup and the resulting data are provided in the main text and supplementary materials. We introduce a microscopic theory of spin-polarized quasiparticle states on superconductors derived from relativistic quantum chemistry methods adapted for vacuum-superconductor systems. This approach enables the calculation of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states at an atomistic level for magnetic adatoms and clusters on superconducting surfaces. By employing a low-order numerical solution for the boundary crossing problem between vacuum and superconductor, we efficiently determine the electronic structure at the atomic scale. We apply this framework to an Mn adatom and dimers/trimers on the W(001)/Nb(110) surface, utilizing a chemically accurate boundary condition. The results align well with experimental data, offering direct insights into the atomic origin of YSR states. Furthermore, the theory predicts that the energy splitting between odd and even YSR peaks for an isolated Mn adatom on Nb(110) can be reversed by coadsorbing a second adatom to form a dimer, a prediction verified experimentally. Additionally, the findings indicate that the spin of an isolated Mn adatom on Nb(110) is not an intrinsic property but rather depends on the local boundary condition at the 3d orbital, a conclusion confirmed by the data. The proposed theory of YSR states provides a valuable tool for investigating magnetic atoms and atoms states on superconducting surfaces. Code access is available at: https://github.com/rajivkumar1975/FRP_YSR.

This study introduces a novel framework for classifying dermoscopic images of skin lesions to identify potential malignant melanomas. The proposed method comprises two primary phases. Initially, an existing convolutional neural network (CNN) model is trained on a dataset containing 10,000 images across five categories: benign, melanoma, and three specific dermatoscopic techniques. To ensure effective multi-class recognition, a simple yet effective outlier detection mechanism is implemented to segment the training data into two distinct groups. In the second phase, two specialized multi-layer perceptron (MLP) classifiers are developed: one to process the majority of samples and another for the remaining outliers. The framework utilizes a state-of-the-art CNN, EfficientNetB0, as the initial feature extractor. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses current methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.49% on the specified dataset. Furthermore, the system exhibits robustness against adversarial attacks, outperforming other contemporary techniques. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Skin-cancer-detection-using-CNN-and-Entropy. This work represents the first application of an outlier detection strategy to derive a balanced dataset for training a CNN, thereby enhancing performance. Additionally, the dual-classifier setup for handling majority and minority data segments shows significant promise for addressing other medical image classification challenges. Ultimately, this methodology offers a reliable solution for diagnosing skin cancer from dermoscopic images and can be extended to various other medical image recognition tasks. At forward angles, the exchange of massive vector bosons in high-energy muon collisions generates a vertex structure that resembles a gluon. This phenomenon, termed the "muon gluon pole," has recently attracted significant attention due to observations of anomalous central gluon rapidity distributions in Drell--Pan muon--nucleus and LAMBA muon--nucleus scattering data. Within the leading-order parton picture, extracting the muon gluon pole distribution function necessitates employing a theoretically robust and computationally efficient formalism. This study derives a concise exact expression for the muon gluon pole, complemented by a computationally streamlined equivalent formulation. We demonstrate that the  "  muon gluon pole  "  represents a genuine high-energy phenomenon, becoming prominent when the center-of-mass energy surpasses the transverse scale under consideration. Furthermore, we establish that this effect is confined to forward scattering and vanishes as the scattering angle approaches ninety degrees. By comparing the exact and approximate formulations of both the gluon pole and W* gamma* vertex functions across various kinematic configurations, we validate the efficacy of the latter. Finally, we contrast the respective contributions of these effects at different kinematic points.

This section of the paper outlines the introduction of a novel family of nonstandard models for the theory of arithmetic, termed the Godel-Carnap-Tarski-Rosser models. These models are constructed by integrating a Godel model, which satisfies the Godel sentence, with a Tarski-Rosser model that interprets the truth predicate in a nonstandard manner. The resulting models are nonstandard and contain a Godelian sentence that the Godel component interprets as true, alongside a nonstandard truth predicate that evaluates this sentence as false. Consequently, these models demonstrate that Godelian sentences and Tarskian truth predicates can be made to fail the Bernays-Levy reflection principle, and they provide counterexamples to the Carnapian principle of necessitarianism for truth predicates. The construction of these Godel-Carnap-Tarski-Rosser models relies on a new variant of the Godelian sentence and the Godel lemma, which is achieved through a modified version of the Godel sentence and Godel theorem by Godel himself. This adaptation involves utilizing a nonstandard truth predicate within the language under consideration, a technique originally proposed by Tarski and later refined by Rosser. Ultimately, this work represents the first instance where a platonistic arithmetic theory has been shown to admit models in which a natural linguistic predicate—specifically, a Godelian sentence—should intuitively be regarded as necessary, yet which violates the Carnapian principle of necessitarianism. The creation of the Godel-Carnap-Tarski-Rosser models serves as the source of conflict for this project, mirroring how Putnam's nonstandard models of set theory caused similar issues in Hilatonian set theory and motivated the development of Kripke's graded K3 semantics for the Tarskian theory of arithmetic with a truth predicate.
